metadata.title: Machine.VM Type Class
metadata.description: A virtual machine, one of the three forms of Machine (CLS-004, by form). Inherits sizing, storage requirements and guest OS from Machine and adds what only a VM has: guest firmware reference, network attachment intent, placement and a desired run state. The hypervisor is the provider, never the type; a Provider Class beneath this carries provider_specific data (CLS-005).

instance_size.description: Provider-neutral size class (small | medium | large, ordered and comparable; common-elements §2.2). Sizes the machine in place of explicit cpu and memory; the provider maps the class to concrete resources at realization. A machine may be declared by size class alone.

count.description: Total virtual CPUs. The provider naturalizes this to its native cpu model (a KubeVirt domain cpu, a hypervisor platform's sockets*cores, a public cloud's vCPUs) at realization (DCM ADR-023).

sockets.description: Optional topology hint: sockets. Provider-support-dependent; ignored where not applicable.

cores_per_socket.description: Optional topology hint: cores per socket. Provider-support-dependent.

cpu.description: As on Machine, with the sub-fields required at this tier.

size.description: Memory allocation, e.g. 16GB or 16Gi (class-aligned quantity pattern — Machine Base Class `memory.size`).

hugepages.description: Optional huge-page backing (provider-support-dependent; validated against provider capability).

memory.description: As on Machine, with the sub-fields required at this tier.

storage.description: Numeric storage requirements the realizing storage must meet — IOPS, throughput, replication, encryption. The performance class is the governed `storage_tier` element, not a value here.

storage_tier.description: The requested storage performance class — a governed `storage_tier` term (standard | performance | archive), each denoting a requirements floor. Name-selectable but requirements-authoritative (ADR-036): a tier name resolves to its floor, explicit `storage` requirements win where both are given, and any provider class that clears the floor qualifies. The provider records the native class it chose as a realized output. Profile decides whether a bare term or a data_reference is required. Governed vocabulary `storage_tier` (ADR-038 §2); name-selectable but requirements-authoritative (ADR-036). Profile decides bare-vs-reference.

disks.description: The machine's disks as portable intent, in order; each entry's `name` is the join key a realized Volume binds to through its `disk_entry`.

boot_order.description: Ordered boot devices: a `disks[].name`, or the device class `network` or `cdrom`.

mounts.description: Network file shares the guest mounts: a FileShare, one of its exports, a mount path, read-only.

source_ref.description: Reference to the FileShare serving the export.

share.description: The export to mount, a `shares[].name` on that FileShare.

mount_path.description: Absolute path in the guest where the share is mounted.

read_only.description: Mount read-only even where the export allows writes.

guest_os.description: The requested operating system, as on Machine; redeclared here so the VM tier may tighten it.

type.description: Inline OS identifier (e.g. linux-server-9). portability_breaking: a value with no os_image vocabulary entry — a review finding.

run_state.description: The run state the consumer wants the provider to drive the machine to (`running`, `stopped`, `suspended`); the provider translates it to its native spec. Observed counterpart: `outputs.observed_run_state`.

firmware.description: Guest firmware: `type` is `legacy` or `uefi` (the Redfish Boot.BootSourceOverrideMode spelling Machine.BareMetalHost shares), plus UEFI Secure Boot and a virtual TPM. Modern guests need uefi + secure_boot + vtpm.

type.description: Firmware interface presented to the guest (Redfish spelling; `legacy` is BIOS).

secure_boot.description: UEFI Secure Boot. Only valid with type: uefi (policy-validated).

vtpm.description: Virtual TPM 2.0 device presented to the guest.

networks.description: Network attachment intent, one entry per interface. An entry may select a network by `network_ref`, or state what it needs (`zone`, `requires`) and let placement choose. Neither is required: unstated, policy decides. Explicit requirements are authoritative over a name, so naming a network that does not meet them is a conflict, not an override. The VM references networks; it never defines segments.

network_ref.description: The VirtualNetwork this interface attaches to — common-elements Reference (handle string or {uuid, handle} object); resolvable, policy-walkable, never an opaque string.

vlan.description: REQUIREMENT — WHICH LOGICAL NETWORK, as a reference to a `VLAN`. The VLAN is the identity of a logical network (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10): a segment id under an encapsulation, which is what an operator means by "put it on that network". Stated when the attachment must land on a specific logical network — because it has to reach something already there, or an existing application lives on it. Absent means policy decides. REALIZATION VARIES; THE AXIS DOES NOT. `VLAN.encapsulation` already carries vlan / vxlan / geneve / flat, so the class is a SEGMENT of which 802.1Q is one form. A public cloud exposes no VLAN — there the segment is a VPC subnet, adopted by reference on VLAN rather than given a parallel class: the VPC is the VirtualNetwork and the subnet is the addressed segment within it. A consumer states the segment; which encapsulation realizes it is the provider's. Resolved against the `segment` relationship a VirtualNetwork already declares, so placement narrows to networks on that segment rather than requiring the consumer to know which provider network carries it.

subnet.description: REQUIREMENT — WHICH IP NETWORK, as a reference to a `Subnet`. Layer 3, and INDEPENDENTLY SELECTABLE from `vlan` (layer 2): a subnet usually sits on a segment, but one segment may carry several subnets and a cloud may expose no segment at all, so the mapping is not concrete (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). "Put me on 198.51.100.0/24" and "put me on VLAN 3020" are different requests; a consumer may state either, both, or neither.

zone.description: REQUIREMENT — the network CATEGORY this attachment needs (DMZ, management, internal), as a governed taxonomy term. Independent of `vlan` and `tier`: which logical network, what kind of network, and how good it is are three different questions, and a consumer may state any, all, or none of them. FOR PLACEMENT ONLY. Requiring the management zone does not grant access to it, and nothing critical may hang off the category directly — anything required because of a zone is enforced by a policy reading it (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). A zero-trust posture derives no trust from network location (NIST SP 800-207).

tier.description: REQUIREMENT — the governed `network_tier` (performance) this attachment needs. Independent of `vlan`: which logical network and how good it is are different questions, and a consumer may state either, both, or neither. Each term denotes a floor, so any network meeting it qualifies — name-selectable but requirements-authoritative (ADR-036).

ip_address_ref.description: A pre-allocated IPAddress to bind to this interface (optional — omitted means the address service allocates at realization). Common-elements Reference shape.

placement.description: Placement intent as a selection of an existing Location, plus affinity relative to other resources. Policy governs which locations a consumer may select; the VM references one, it never defines locations.

location_ref.description: Reference to an existing Location the VM is placed in — chosen from the eligible set (platform-layer + provider-advertised, policy-filtered). Also carried as a references->Location relationship.

zone.description: Availability/sovereignty zone constraint, selected from the zones the provider advertises for the chosen location; resolved against that location.

affinity.description: Co-location / separation intent relative to OTHER named resources (not nodes). Each target is resolved at reserve, so a pre-known UUID is not required.

target.description: The resources to co-locate with or avoid, as a URF filter (identifier-scheme §9) — a handle such as `cexample/vms/web-01`, or a selector such as `estate?labels.tier==web`. Resolved at reserve (DCM ADR-025/AEP-124), so you do not need a UUID in advance.

selector.description: Alternative to a handle: match target(s) by labels (key/value).

spec.description: Deliberate exclusions: GPU/PCI passthrough and SR-IOV are Provider-Class SharedDataElements (ADR-038) — provider-variable capability, not portable base surface. Day-0 guest personalization (cloud-init/user-data) is an open design decision (process concern vs VM field) — tracked on the type, not silently absent. Per-disk shape (sizes, roles) is the `disks` element on Machine.

realized_volumes.description: DERIVED: per-disk realization map, items {entry, volume, storage_backing}. For each `disks[].name`, the Volume realizing it (by the volume's `realizes_disk` edge and `disk_entry` join key) and the native storage class the provider chose, the ADR-036 realized fact behind the entry's `storage_tier`. Computed from the Volume records, never stored (compute-never-store); the lineage surface from declared disk to realized volume.

observed_run_state.description: The run state the provider last observed, normalized to the same vocabulary as `run_state` (Redfish PowerState On and Off, a KubeVirt phase, an HMC partition state all land here; PoweringOn and PoweringOff are `transitioning`). Drives shutdown and startup ordering for the dependency graph. One output for every form of Machine (row 111).

provider_handle.description: The provider-native identifier of the realized VM (opaque; correlation/ops use only — never a portable reference).

primary_ip.description: The primary/management address — first of ip_addresses; the single-address convenience most bindings want.

hostname.description: Realized guest hostname (FQDN where the realm provides one).

ip_addresses.description: Assigned guest IP addresses (all interfaces), IPv4-first ordering. The canonical binding surface for LB backend pools, DNS records, and monitoring targets.

mac_addresses.description: Realized MAC per interface, ordered as spec.networks[]. Binding surface for DHCP reservation and switch-port records.

target_segment.description: Realize-time placement fact (ADR-011 two-phase reserve): a reference to the VLAN segment the reserved/realized placement can reach (adopt-not-absorb — the segment id/encapsulation live on the VLAN). This is the declarable binding source for a fulfillment:provider dependency whose criteria are simply the target segment — e.g. a IPAddress allocated on the reachable segment (DCM ADR-009 §3 worked example: bind target_segment -> the IP request's segment_ref). It is a shared-reference fact, NOT the vNIC/MAC/host-networking (those are the VM provider's own internal facts, never cross-provider criteria).

relationships.name: mounts
relationships.description: Declared on the machine: its guest mounts an export of this FileShare (spec.mounts names which). The consumer declares the edge, so a share never lists the machines that mount it.
May consume zero or more pre-allocated IPAddress addresses (optional dependency).

relationships.name: placement
relationships.description: Placed in an existing Location (selected, policy-governed) — see spec.placement.location_ref.

relationships.name: network_attachment
relationships.description: Attaches to existing VirtualNetwork(s) — see spec.networks[].network_ref.

relationships.name: disk
relationships.description: Consumes existing/allocated Volume(s) — the consumable volumes realizing its `disks` entries.

adopts.role: Vendor-neutral compute-system representation spanning physical, virtual and partitioned (Redfish ComputerSystem SystemType: Physical | Virtual | Composed | PhysicallyPartitioned | VirtuallyPartitioned) — the one representative standard for the Machine family, shared by Machine.VM, Machine.BareMetalHost and Machine.LPAR and declared once here. Nova with Ironic, Cluster API's Machine and TOSCA's Compute are the industry abstractions that treat the three forms as one thing (CLS-002 (a)); Redfish is the wire representation adopted. Provider-native realizations are declared on the provider support matrix, not on the substrate type.
mount field names for `mounts` (mountPath, readOnly), snake_case, shared with UDLM's Container `mounts`
k8s-native VM realization vocabulary (domain cpu/memory, interfaces->networks, volumes, runStrategy/power) — the parallel to Metal3 for bare metal

context.purpose: Declares a virtual machine — sizing, guest OS, storage requirements, network attachments, placement — as portable intent any virtualization provider can realize.
context.plain_description: The request for one VM: how big — a named size class (`instance_size`), or explicit `cpu` and `memory` in its place — what `guest_os`, what storage it needs (`storage` minima and a governed `storage_tier`), which disks it has (`disks`, on Machine), and which existing networks its NICs attach to (`networks`, each entry naming a `network_ref`). Placement is a selection of an existing location, not an invention. Once the provider builds it, the record carries realized facts back: IP addresses, hostname, provider handle. The hypervisor (KubeVirt, libvirt, a cloud) is a provider detail, never part of the type.
use_when: You need to request a VM with declared size, OS, storage requirements, and network attachments, portable across hypervisors.
You need VM records in the dependency graph so ordering (host before VM, VM before its services) is derivable.
You need a VM's addresses to reference existing IPAddress records rather than duplicate them.
not_for: The physical machine it runs on — Machine.BareMetalHost.
A containerized workload — Container; the VM carries a full guest OS.
The vNIC as a device record — that is NetworkInterface with a virtual device_class; the VM's networks list declares attachment intent, not device inventory.
works_with: VirtualNetwork — the networks the VM's NICs attach to.
Volume — the consumable volumes realizing its `disks` entries.
Location — where the VM is placed (selected from existing places, policy-governed).
IPAddress — pre-allocated addresses the VM consumes.
